items.content:
Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady as midterm elections loom
The Fed raised interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month.
The Federal Reserve held interest rates steady on Wednesday as the economy faces a monthslong surge of inflation ahead of the midterm elections.
The Fed's benchmark interest rate currently stands between 3.75% and 4%. That level marks a significant drop from a recent peak attained in 2023, but rates stand well above a 0% level established at the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic.
An acceleration of price increases this year has posed a challenge for Fed officials tasked with containing inflation. The central bank raised interest rates a quarter of a percentage point last month in an effort to battle back price woes. The move marked the first rate increase in three years.
That rate hike should help cool off inflation by slowing the economy and eating away at demand, though such a policy move typically yields results after a lag time lasting several months.
Prices increased 3.7% in September compared to a year earlier, putting the inflation rate more than a percentage point above the Fed's target level of 2%, data showed.
Speaking at a press conference in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said policymakers had opted to leave rates unchanged as they await further economic data.
"The committee believes the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2% goal," Warsh said.
Warsh voiced optimism about U.S. economic performance, even as he acknowledged the challenge posed by elevated inflation.
"Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient," Warsh said.
Control of Congress is up for grabs on Election Day. What's the math for Democrats and Republicans?
Policymakers may lose patience as they weigh whether the current level of interest rates is high enough to ease price hikes. The odds of a quarter-point rate hike at the Fed's next meeting in December are pegged at nearly 80%, according to CME Group's FedWatch Tool , a measure of market sentiment.
In the meantime, price increases are accelerating. Inflation rose to a four-month high in September as fuel prices climbed in response to unrest in the Middle East, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
The rise of inflation may put pressure on the Fed to ratchet up interest rates in an escalation of its fight against price hikes. That policy would mean pressing the brakes harder on the economy -- risking sluggish growth and job cuts.
US Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh attends the IMF/World Bank 2026 Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, October 16, 2026.
Warsh also announced plans for the Fed to issue just seven rate decisions in 2027 compared to eight this year.

Federal judge rules top US prosecutor in Los Angeles isn't legally serving
In 2028, the Fed plans to reduce the number of rate decisions to six, Warsh said.
"Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular and information-rich intervals. But it’s equally important we reserve time and space as an intellectually diverse group for strategic deliberations," he added.
A weak jobs report this month complicated the economic picture, suggesting a resilient labor market may be wobbling more than previously thought.
Employers added 29,000 jobs in September, a sharp slowdown from the 162,000 jobs added in August, the BLS said. The job gains came in well below economists' expectations.
Economic conditions pose a quandary for the Fed, Bank of America Global Research said in a memo to clients last week.
"If the Fed hikes, investors might worry about overtightening. If the Fed holds, markets could question the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility," the memo said.
The rate decision may also thrust the central bank into a political maelstrom in the final sprint to Election Day.
President Donald Trump has repeatedly criticized the Fed for raising interest rates over across both terms in office, including a reprimand leveled at the Fed soon after its rate increase last month.
"LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!" Trump said in a social media post hours after the announcement.

The Fed is an independent institution established by Congress. The central bank is typically insulated from political interference, but several past presidents have sought to influence the Fed’s interest rate policy, including Trump.
The rate decision may also draw attention to the challenge posed by inflation, a top issue among voters.
In a memo to clients before the rate announcement, Deutsche Bank Research said the upcoming midterms could factor into a potential decision to hold interest rates steady, though in their view the election would not be a "primary consideration."
"We could imagine that all else equal the Fed might prefer to stay out of the headlines for raising rates just ahead of a midterm election where affordability is the principal concern," the memo said.

Share Fed leaves interest rates unchanged despite inflation in the US on social media
The decision by the US Federal Reserve, the central bank in the United States, comes less than a week before the country's midterm elections [File: Ken Cedeno/Reuters]
The United States Federal Reserve is set to hold interest rates steady in its final monetary policy decision before the US midterm elections.
The central bank will maintain rates at 3.75-4 percent, following a 10-2 vote, in line with expectations.

CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, indicated that there was more than a 90 percent chance rates would remain unchanged.
“Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace,” the Fed said in its press release announcing the decision on Wednesday. “While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient. Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment is robust. Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.”
It also added, “The accumulation of more information will help the Committee determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the Committee’s 2 percent goal.”
The most recent Consumer Price Index (CPI) report showed the annual inflation rate increasing to 3.7 percent in September , up from 3.4 percent in August, with energy prices largely accounting for the monthly surge.
There were signs earlier this month that the central bank would maintain benchmark interest rates, with the Fed’s chair for supervision, Michelle Bowman, advocating a “wait and see” approach.
“I don’t feel any urgency for taking further action at this point,” she said at this month’s International Monetary Fund-World Bank meetings in Bangkok, Thailand. “We really need to take some time and understand how things will evolve.”
The decision comes before Thursday’s release of the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) Price Index report, which is used by the central bank to assess inflation and inform its decisions.
Today’s Fed announcement follows an interest-rate hike rise last month, amid surging inflation – the first increase by the central bank since July 2023. The move drew criticism from US President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly pressed the Fed to cut rates since taking office. At the time, he wrote on Truth Social that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less.”
The Fed’s next monetary policy meeting is scheduled for December 8-9, when it will give its final rate decision of the year.
Current forecasts point to a quarter-point interest rate increase.

items.title: Microsoft Maia 300: Could Its New AI Chip Challenge NVIDIA? - Cloud Wars
items.summary: Microsoft Maia 300: Could Its New AI Chip Challenge NVIDIA?  Cloud Wars
items.content:
In today’s Cloud Wars Minute, I analyze Microsoft’s ambitious Maia 300 rollout and how owning its own AI chips could give the company greater control over its AI infrastructure, improve efficiency, and reduce its reliance on NVIDIA.
00:10 — Microsoft has announced Maia 300 , the company's latest custom AI chip. It's also revealed plans to expand its Azure Maia systems to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, and with this rollout, Maia will become the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services.
01:02 — Microsoft expects Maia 300 to deliver 40% more tokens per megawatt than leading GPU-based systems. In other words, Microsoft expects to deliver more AI output for the same amount of power. That's crucial as demand for AI services continues to skyrocket. Now, Microsoft also says that in a full configuration, Maia 300 systems are expected to deliver up to seven times the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.
01:41 — Bear in mind that Maia 200 is already a very capable system, and Maia 300 really builds on those foundations — I'm going to quote Microsoft here: "To enable more coding with GitHub, more flexible AI model deployment through Microsoft Foundry, and faster interactions with Copilot, Teams, and Dragon Copilot." Now, back to that incredibly important point I made at the start.
02:05 — Maia is set to become the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services. Now, back in August, I talked about what this could mean for NVIDIA. My conclusion was that Microsoft's own chips could help level the playing field and give the company more options.
02:33 — Could Microsoft chips potentially challenge NVIDIA in the market? I think that remains to be seen. Microsoft's announcement certainly seems to suggest that it will have more control over its AI infrastructure , but it doesn't necessarily mean that NVIDIA is being pushed out of the picture altogether. What is clear, though, is that Microsoft is moving towards a much more full-circle AI business with its own chips, cloud infrastructure, models, and applications.

items.title: OpenAI Is Buying Google’s AI Chips, a Hit to Nvidia’s Biggest Customer Bond - 24/7 Wall St.
items.summary: OpenAI Is Buying Google’s AI Chips, a Hit to Nvidia’s Biggest Customer Bond  24/7 Wall St.
items.content:
OpenAI Is Buying Google’s AI Chips, a Hit to Nvidia’s Biggest Customer Bond
OpenAI reportedly buying Google's custom AI chips would quietly shift leverage in one of the most lucrative vendor relationships in tech, and the fallout for NVIDIA's pricing power and Alphabet's chip ambitions is only beginning to take shape.
The symbolic act of connecting to an AI processing unit highlights the critical role of specialized chips in advancing artificial intelligence, mirroring the recent strategic shifts in the tech industry. © 24/7 Wall St.
OpenAI has spent more on NVIDIA ( NASDAQ:NVDA | NVDA Price Prediction ) graphics processors than almost any other company, and it now plans to buy Google's own AI chips, according to The Information. The report came out the night of October 27, 2026. It cites one person familiar with the matter and mentions Google's tensor processing units (TPUs), custom chips built for AI work.
Neither company has confirmed the plan. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment, and OpenAI declined to comment.
Alphabet  ( NASDAQ:GOOG , NASDAQ:GOOGL ) closed at $320.58, up 1.19%, a gain of $3.78, and then added 0.93% after hours to reach $323.57. NVIDIA rose 0.9% to $217.94 and stayed nearly flat after hours at $218.14.
No terms, volumes, timing, or chip generation have been disclosed. Until one of the companies confirms it, this remains a reported plan, since nobody has shown a signed order.
OpenAI has used TPUs before. It began renting Google's AI chips in June 2025, and the report adds that it now owns them. A year earlier, OpenAI said it had "no specific plans to use TPUs at present."
OpenAI has been moving in this direction for a while. It recently said it would offer its frontier models through Google Cloud. In June, it announced its first custom chip, and a current job listing asks for "significant experience optimizing real workloads on TPUs for training or inference."
A buyer this large wants a second supplier because it gains leverage on price, protection against supply shortages, and software that is not tied to a single vendor.
Alphabet started selling TPUs directly to some customers this year, although its chief financial officer has said most of that revenue will be recognized in 2027. Google already rents TPUs to Anthropic, Apple ( NASDAQ:AAPL ) and Citadel Securities. An OpenAI purchase would show that TPUs can work as a chip business selling to outside buyers, on top of a cloud unit whose revenue grew 82% to $24.77 billion last quarter.
For NVIDIA, the first measure is scale: its data center unit brought in $89.02 billion in a single quarter. Its financial ties to OpenAI are also extensive. On August 17, 2026, NVIDIA agreed to provide up to $105 billion in credit support for an OpenAI data center in Ohio that starts at 4.25 gigawatts. NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang reportedly said OpenAI committed to spend about $600 billion on NVIDIA servers through 2030.
OpenAI still calls itself one of NVIDIA's biggest customers. On the same day as the report, its computing chief said, in a joint announcement with NVIDIA and Oracle ( NYSE:ORCL ), "We are bringing Vera into production on OCI to support these workloads at scale."
Huang has said he is "very confident that they're going to be customers and partners of ours for a very long time." As the seller, he would naturally say that, but no evidence shows OpenAI cutting its orders.
The risk to NVIDIA is a slow loss of pricing power, because each credible alternative improves the buyer's position in negotiations. NVIDIA trades at a price-to-earnings ratio of 44, and that multiple assumes NVIDIA keeps its 71.1% gross margin. TPU software still lags behind NVIDIA's, so the purchase could be smaller or slower than the headline implies.
Alphabet has fallen 5.79% over the past week and is up only 2.62% this year, while NVIDIA is up 17.13%.
At a P/E of 14 and a market value of $3.874 trillion, Alphabet costs far less than NVIDIA at $5.263 trillion. That gap suggests the market gives little premium to Alphabet's position as a credible second AI chip supplier.
The next test comes when Alphabet reports after the close on October 28, 2026. If management names outside TPU buyers or raises its 2027 TPU revenue outlook, the case gets stronger. If the call skips TPUs and the stock closes below $320.58, the market will have viewed this report as noise.
Contact [email protected] for any questions or corrections.
Omor Ibne Ehsan is a writer at 24/7 Wall St. He is a self-taught investor with a focus on growth, cyclical, and dividend equities that have strong fundamentals, value, and long-term potential. He also has an interest in high-risk, high-reward investments such as penny stocks.

items.title: High-speed train crash kills at least 68 people in Spain
items.summary: The crash, between a moving train and another that was stopped further up the track, was caused by an "inexplicable" error, the transport minister said.
items.content:
Figure caption, Watch: 'Chaotic scenes' at site of Spain's deadly train crash
A high-speed train crash has killed at least 68 people and injured dozens more in central Spain.
It occurred when a train travelling from Madrid to Seville barrelled into another train - which was stationary on the tracks - on Wednesday morning. The force saw several carriages fall down an embankment.
The transport minister said a computer failure followed by human error caused the crash, which is one of the worst in Europe's modern history, and Spain's deadliest train disaster in 13 years.
Survivors described harrowing scenes of passengers being thrown into the air, trapped in the wreckage and smashing windows to get out.
The crash happened just after 09:00 (08:00 GMT) around 140km (87 miles) south of Madrid, between the municipalities of Mora and Orgaz.
The stationary train, run by private rail operator Iryo, had 147 passengers on board, and had stopped on the tracks because of a computer failure, Spain's Transport Minister Ãscar Puente said.
He explained that when there is a system failure, a 24-hour control centre in Madrid takes over, but it had made an "inexplicable" decision to instruct the trains to move again, without any speed restrictions.
Iryo said its train was "struck from behind" by another train, run by Spain's state-owned railway company, Renfe, which was carrying 397 passengers.
The force of the crash was "brutal", said 62-year-old passenger Salvador Arriza who was sitting in the Renfe-operated train.
Passengers started breaking the windows to get out, he told Reuters, adding that "some people couldn't move because they were trapped amongst the seats."
One of the carriages caught fire, and passengers described devastating scenes of trapped people crying and bleeding, with some buried under debris.
Pictures show that a long piece of railway track had speared through one of the carriages.
Image caption, The force of the crash saw several carriage fall down an embankment
Tangui Binier, 22, was on the Iryo train and told the BBC that "suitcases started flying and people were screaming" when the train finally came to a halt.
There was a lot of smoke and confusion, he said, and described seeing the train "completely flipped over" when he stepped outside.
"It was hard to witness", Binier said, adding that his father carried a girl who had a broken hip out of the wreckage.
He also described seeing dead bodies and missing limbs: "I don't know if I'll ever recover."
Image caption, Some passengers said the piece of train track that speared through a carriage may have slowed the train down
Spanish journalist Antonio JimÃ©nez Barca, who works for El Pais newspaper, was walking to the Renfe train's cafeteria when the crash happened.
"I felt like I was being pushed from behind, like I was being thrown to the ground," he described.
"I hit my head horribly... I was covered in blood. There were people on top of me. One person had an injured arm, and another had a head injury."
Another passenger, 46-year-old SebastiÃ¡n Herrero, told El Mundo newspaper that he saw "many people with broken noses, broken arms."
"It was a terrible, terrible impact," he said, adding that he was "in the air for about four or five seconds," which felt like a lifetime.
Many of the passengers said they were in shock, and one sobbed during an interview with a local television station as he described a woman dying in his arms.
"She was very cold and she was all alone," he said, to which the show's presenter also started to cry.
Dozens of ambulances rushed to the scene, and a helicopter evacuated those with the most serious injuries.
Spain's Civil Guard said it would need DNA samples from relatives to identify some victims.
"The whole of Spain is grieving", Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez said during a visit to the crash site. "Lives have been shattered, families have been torn apart, the pain is immense."
Spain was already reeling from a high-speed rail disaster near CÃ³rdoba in January that killed 46 people. It happened on the same rail line, but much further south.
Wednesday's crash is the worst the country has seen since 2013, when when 80 people died on the outskirts of Santiago de Compostela in north-west Spain.
"Spain has the right to know what is happening with its infrastructure," said Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o, leader of the the main opposition People's Party.
Spanish trade union CSIF has demanded the transport minister resign, accusing him of "scapegoating" a traffic manager, by blaming human error in the control room, instead of "taking responsibility".
SÃ¡nchez and other Spanish politicians cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
The prime minister said it was "unacceptable" for Spain to have two serious train crashes in one year, and vowed to "get to the bottom of this" and determine if there was any negligence.
"If there have been failures in the security system, they will be addressed with the utmost firmness."

items.content:
China Is Building Its Way Around Europe’s EV Tariffs
Beijing’s evolving industrial playbook is taking shape in Morocco.
By Aaron Glasserman , a distinguished fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University and a fellow on foreign policy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis, and Jessie Jiexi Lin , a student pursuing a master’s in public administration at Columbia University’s School of International and Public Affairs.
Workers in dark uniforms and blue baseball caps inspect the metal frames of silver, unpainted electric vehicles along a brightly lit assembly line on a factory floor. The line of cars extends backward to the far wall, with similar small groups of workers bustling around each one.
Workers check vehicle frames on the production line for electric vehicle maker Zeekr at its factory in Ningbo, China, on May 29, 2025. Kevin Frayer/Getty Images
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
In recent years, Europe’s auto industry has reeled from the influx of low-cost, high-quality Chinese electric vehicles (EVs). Even as Brussels imposes tariffs on Chinese-made EVs, their market share only continues to grow. As of December, more than 9 percent of all new automobiles sold in Europe were made in China, with some estimates expecting Chinese EVs to account for roughly 20 percent of the Western European market by 2028.
Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs reflect a common Western view that high-value Chinese products are competitive in global markets largely because of state subsidies . To be sure, China’s EV industry has benefited immensely from Beijing’s subsidies, easy credit, and tax relief. That explanation, however, is far too narrow and risks severely underestimating the scale of the challenge ahead.
The more consequential story—that will likely make Chinese EVs even more competitive in the near future—is Beijing’s evolving approach to overseas industrial policy. At the core of this approach is an increasingly coordinated model of public- and private-sector activity.
State-owned enterprises (SOE) lay the groundwork for favorable investment environments abroad by undertaking massive infrastructure projects and securing access to strategic resources. Boosted by Beijing’s diplomatic ties and international clout, private companies leverage these state-backed platforms as a springboard for trade by bringing in investment, production capacity, and industry-specific expertise.
The advantages of this approach for Beijing—and the challenge that it poses to foreign companies—are already on full display in Morocco, where years of existing strategic investment, infrastructure development, and geopolitical maneuvering are pushing China closer to vertically integrating EV supply chains, bypassing tariffs, and further reshaping Europe’s auto industry.
It is only in recent years that Morocco has emerged as a key node in China’s EV empire.
For decades, Beijing maintained much closer ties with Morocco’s neighbor and rival, Algeria, but that began to change in the early 2010s as the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) took off. In 2016, Morocco joined the growing ranks of countries signing “strategic partnerships” with China, making mutual commitments to expand economic cooperation and recognize each other’s core interests.
The next year, Morocco officially entered the BRI, and China has since poured millions of dollars into Morocco’s energy and transportation sectors . Almost a decade later, that economic relationship has expanded dramatically: In March, China’s committed investment in the country exceeded $10 billion , concentrated mostly in the EV and energy sectors.
China’s EV manufacturing capacity in Morocco builds on years of large-scale, state-backed investment in transportation infrastructure and natural resources. Over the past decade, Chinese SOEs have collaborated on major infrastructure and development projects in Morocco, including bridges , highways , and smart cities . Some of these are directly relevant to the EV industry, such as the chemical processing unit in Khouribga, home to one of the world’s biggest reserves of phosphate, which is critical for EV battery production .
This SOE-led scramble for resources and construction-heavy projects paved the way for private Chinese companies in the EV sector to establish footholds in Morocco and ship to overseas markets. Tanger Tech City, China’s SOE-led flagship collaboration with Morocco, is located less than 30 miles from Tanger Med, the largest container port in Africa. Taking advantage of no-fee business registration and tax-free dividends, private Chinese companies—including the global battery giant BTR New Material Group as well as tire manufacturers Sentury Tire and Guizhou Tyre—have established or announced plans to establish production bases in the industrial zone.
Elsewhere in the country, major private investments include battery manufacturer Gotion’s $1.3 billion factory and a $2 billion joint-venture battery materials factory between China’s CNGR Advanced Material and the Moroccan private equity firm Al Mada.
This isn’t to deny the role of subsidies and preferential financing, which Beijing sees as key tools for supporting companies that are expanding internationally. A 2024 directive , for instance, called on Chinese financial institutions to improve credit approval and lending procedures and to enhance cross-border settlement to “better support companies expanding into international markets.” Closer collaboration among Chinese banks, semi-official trade organizations, and Moroccan banks has also helped to streamline financing and channel investment into the African market.
But these policies are useful to Chinese firms because they are operating in an industrial landscape that SOEs have already shaped, with relatively easy access to necessary resources and infrastructure.
China’s success with this approach has only been possible because it also advances Rabat’s desire to expand domestic manufacturing capability and position Morocco as Africa’s next industrial powerhouse. Chinese investment is expected to generate sorely needed jobs; Morocco’s unemployment rate has hardly dipped below 10 percent for the past decade, and youth unemployment in cities stands at a staggering 47 percent. Officials claim that the Gotion factory alone will create 17,000 local jobs, including 2,300 high-skilled positions.
Beijing has coupled this economic engagement with a subtle diplomatic shift in favor of Rabat’s claims over Western Sahara . For decades, China has avoided explicitly backing either Morocco or Western Sahara, though its rhetoric often leaned toward the latter—and thus to the latter’s main sponsor, Algiers . With one exception in 2018, it consistently voted in favor of United Nations Security Council resolutions extending the peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara and affirming support for the Sahrawi people’s right to self-determination.
However, in recent years, China has done an about-face. In 2024, its Ministry of Foreign Affairs implicitly acknowledged the importance of the Western Sahara question for Rabat, stating , “China supports Morocco in maintaining national security and stability and is ready to work with Morocco to continue firmly supporting each other on issues concerning their respective core interests.” Then, last fall, Beijing abstained on the most recent U.N. resolution on the matter, which for the first time endorsed Rabat’s proposal to formally establish Western Sahara as an autonomous region under Moroccan sovereignty.
The full payoff of China’s Moroccan gambit will materialize if and when localized EV manufacturing matures, which could take years. That is still a tall order, as evidenced by the recent shelving of a BYD assembly plant project that had been stalled since 2017 due to budget issues and limited local charging infrastructure, according to a company executive.
Though Chinese automakers are not yet building assembly plants in Morocco, the country matters for everything “upstream” of assembly. It is becoming an integrated ecosystem for the production of batteries, tires, and other components, which reduces Chinese EV companies’ reliance on direct shipments from China and lowers costs for Chinese assembly plants in Europe and Africa.
Morocco also offers Chinese firms convenient access to the European market through the Tanger Med port and—more importantly—a rules-based pathway through Brussels’s tightening trade defenses . Currently, the EU imposes duties of up to 35 percent on EVs manufactured in China. However, vehicles that qualify as Moroccan in origin can enter the European market duty-free. That includes vehicles assembled in Morocco, so long as foreign parts make up less than 45 percent of the finished vehicle’s ex-works price.
In short, if Chinese EV companies succeed in establishing vehicle assembly factories and fully integrating supply chains in Morocco, they will be able to sell vehicles to Europe under a “Made in Morocco” label, avoiding both the 10 percent EU standard automobile tariff and the additional punitive tariff on Chinese-made EVs—reducing the total tariff effect from as much as 45 percent to zero. This would pose an unprecedented threat to what remains one of the EU’s most important industries .
China is rolling out this coordinated approach to overseas industrial policy elsewhere to varying degrees.
In Thailand, for example, China is a key investor in the Eastern Economic Corridor, a flagship regional development initiative anchored by a high-speed railway that will connect several Thai cities and seaports to China. The corridor has, in turn, provided an attractive environment for private Chinese investment. China is now the corridor’s largest source of foreign direct investment, primarily in the EV sector and related industries. Like Tanger Tech City, the corridor offers private Chinese companies major tax incentives and more convenient access to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations’ market.
The United Arab Emirates offers another example. In 2017, Chinese SOE Jiangsu Provincial Overseas Cooperation and Investment Company Limited (JOCIC) partnered with Abu Dhabi Ports to develop an industrial and special economic zone inside the Khalifa Port’s free trade zone. JOCIC set up a wholly owned UAE subsidiary to manage the park, which lets it attract Chinese private capital while insulating the parent company from project-level and geopolitical risk. The park’s location provides Chinese companies with a convenient base for expansion into the Persian Gulf and wider Middle Eastern markets, along with exemptions from value-added tax and other financial incentives . As of 2025, more than 40 Chinese companies had collectively committed more than $700 million to the park, with a focus on EVs and renewable energy.
Beijing has long seen its SOEs as tools for advancing its broader economic interests. As China in recent years has emphasized “small and beautiful” projects , the SOE-led megaprojects are often viewed as commercially disappointing holdovers from an earlier and more profligate era of BRI. Nevertheless, under this coordinated strategy, Beijing has been able to capitalize on the advantages secured by past infrastructure projects and deepen its presence in the overseas market.
As governments in industrialized economies respond to China’s surge of high-value manufactured exports, they must recognize how the sources of Chinese firms’ advantages are changing. Today, those advantages come not just from subsidies and cheap credit at home but also from integrated ecosystems abroad, built through coordination between public and private enterprise.
This means that Brussels’s retaliatory tariffs and the recently announced limits on hybrid EVs imported from China, on their own, are unlikely to stem the tide of EVs made by Chinese firms operating around the world. China’s rivals—even in industrialized economies—will struggle to compete unless they can coordinate across borders and build supply chains and infrastructure that leverage or, far less plausibly, completely sidestep what China has already put in place.
Aaron Glasserman is a distinguished fellow at the Weatherhead East Asian Institute at Columbia University and a fellow on foreign policy at the Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis.

Rescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images
Rescue workers at the site of Wednesday’s rail disaster in Spain’s Toledo province. A high-speed service hit another train halted by a signalling fault. Photograph: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/Getty Images
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%
Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long been a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety.
Officials said at least 68 people were killed on Wednesday morning after a high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were believed to be carrying 544 passengers.
Speaking to reporters, Spain’s transport minister, Óscar Puente, traced the collision back to a security system that had stopped working at about 8.30am local time. The computer malfunction brought an estimated six trains to a halt along a 63km stretch of track.
Soon after, the central command in Madrid instructed one of the trains involved in the crash to resume service at normal speeds, sending it colliding into a train that was still sitting stationary on the tracks, said Puente. “It was the control centre – via its operators – that made the decision to resume operations, under circumstances that, from our point of view, are inexplicable,” he added .
State-owned rail operator Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”.
The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.
A Guardia Civil officer collects evidence at the site of January’s fatal rail crash near Adamuz in Andalucía. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network.
The first crash sparked conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued.
Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month.
Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.”
map It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo.
The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport.
While the causes of the January crash remain under investigation, a preliminary report suggested that it could have been the result of defects in the track or in a weld between two sections of track. The report noted, however, that several other possibilities were also being investigated.
Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain.
The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018.
The aftermath of the 2013 crash near Santiago de Compostela that claimed 80 lives. Photograph: Reuters Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU.
Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.
Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.
Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU.
On Wednesday, Spain’s prime minister said measures would be taken to rebuild trust in the country’s high-speed rail system. “Because it is simply unacceptable for a country like Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in the same year, as we have,” said Sánchez.
The crash was Spain’s worst rail accident since 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

items.title: Dharshini David: Healey buys himself some time, but big questions still unanswered
items.summary: The chancellor talked of charting a new course for Britain, but the impact of Iran war has limited his options.
items.content:
Image caption, While earnings are rising, forecasters predict that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes
John Healey talked of charting a new course for Britain, but this Budget was more about course-correcting than charging down a new path.
It was abundantly clear that the financial fallout from that conflict in the Middle East has hampered the finances of households and businesses â and the government's ability to help.
While the government targeted those impacted by higher energy and fuel bills, the "breathing space" it aimed to provide was limited; it is a pill that doesn't fully alleviate the pain.
The most telling evidence was that official forecasters predict that while earnings will rise, that is not compensating for higher prices and taxes.
Even after the extra help is taken into account, households' incomes after inflation and tax are set to be typically lower across the next two years than the start of the parliament. On that basis, it could be the second worse parliament for living standards, after the last one, since the 1950s - a sign of how far the war has blown prosperity off course.
But it can't be all be blamed on the war. Taxes haven't helped. Although there were few major measures aimed at households, the policy of previous chancellors of freezing the thresholds at which different rates of tax on income apply - fiscal drag - has been maintained in the background, scooping more money out of pay packets.
Overall, this Budget has the tax burden - the proportion of the nation's income going to the tax office - rising to a new historic high of 38.6%
However, a more generous package of help would have been hard to pull off. The impact of higher inflation and debt have increased borrowing costs by Â£14bn in the past year alone.
The Chancellor had to prove to the markets which lend the government money that he has a plan to bring down future debt to avoid those costs climbing further.
As it stands, debt interest repayments are due to be Â£160bn in 2032, more than double the amount spent on schools in England.
And the plans Healey has unveiled already eat into wiggle room he has within the public finances. He says he was right to do so - that's what such safety margins are there for - in times of strife. But the great uncertainty that remains made going further very risky. Energy prices remaining high, for example, could easily chew up all the spare cash.
So the result was what some have termed a beige, safe Budget. As Healey strove to prove his fiscally sound credentials, there wasn't even the customary rabbit pulled out of the hat, the end-of-speech sweetener.
The markets seem reassured â even if some of his tax raising plans involve clamping down on loopholes and those not paying the right tax, which is always highly uncertain.
Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
So the chancellor appears to have bought himself some breathing space. But that means some big questions have been postponed until another day, not least on public services.
Higher-than-expected inflation may mean that if areas such as health and defence are prioritised, budgets for some other "unprotected" areas â justice and higher education for example â are set to lag behind inflation after 2028.
There was a hint too from John Healey that he'd tap into some of those budgets to help out defence spending. To maintain those budgets in 2030 would means finding tens of billions of pounds.
And issues around the other big area of spending â welfare â remain unresolved. Between 2025 and 2032, spending there is set to increase by Â£100bn.
The official forecasters also noted the rapid rise in sickness and disability caseloads since the start of the pandemic. They warn if that trend continued, spending on such benefits would rise by a further Â£13bn.
Any suggestion of welfare reform has been postponed until the forthcoming review into the plight of workless young people.
Then there's the issue of boosting growth. There was a bit more detail on the plans for devolution â but there is much to be fleshed out.
And on another key part of the growth strategy, housebuilding, there was disappointing news. Even though first-time buyers are set to get more help, their first home may be more elusive.
Between regulation and higher costs â in part, related to the war - the OBR estimates that 190,000 fewer homes will be built by 2032 compared to what it thought in March, a significant setback.
So the chancellor may have unveiled 98 (relatively small) measures but the to-do list gets longer.
With his official forecasters warning that, in a very uncertain world, his finances face exceptional risks, playing a wait-and-see game feels like a prudent move.
The risks go both ways: the OBR points out that a swift resolution to the war and an improvement in the economy could spell a significant boost to the public finances.
So the chancellor has more reason than most to keep his fingers crossed that happens rapidly.
For as it stands, the official forecasters say incomes after inflation, living standards, are set to be only 1% higher at the end of the decade than at the start.
A series of economic shocks outside out control could thwart plans to turbo-boost prosperity . And as today shows, breathing space only extends so far.

By Al Jazeera Staff , Reuters and The Associated Press
European countries will not be included in the next round of talks with Ukraine and the United States planned to take place in Abu Dhabi, according to a top foreign policy aide at the Kremlin.
Interfax news agency quoted Yuri Ushakov, who said the possible participation of European countries was not discussed during a  90-minute phone call on Tuesday among Russian President Vladimir Putin, Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store.

But Stubb offered a different account, telling a meeting of the Nordic Council in Helsinki that European countries would be involved in November’s Abu Dhabi talks.
Speaking at a news conference in the Netherlands on Wednesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said trilateral talks with Russia and the US would take place from November 6 to November 10 in the United Arab Emirates.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv wanted Europe to also be involved in the talks, adding that unity and stronger pressure on Russia were needed.
His comments came after he met with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, who pledged an extra 500 million euros ($556m) for military support to Ukraine this winter to buy drones and other material to strengthen Ukraine’s defences. Zelenskyy is also due to meet Dutch King Willem-Alexander on Wednesday.
Earlier in the day before Zelenskyy’s visit, the Dutch government announced a new support package for Ukraine worth 1.2 billion euros ($1.33bn) over the next three years and a contribution of 40 million euros ($44.5m) by the end of this year to the Ukraine Energy Support Fund.
“Support for recovery and reconstruction can’t wait for a ceasefire. Ukraine needs our help right now – military support but also social and economic assistance,” Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Dutch minister for foreign trade and development cooperation, said during a visit to Kyiv on Wednesday.
“However successful you are on the battlefield, it’s also essential that energy systems, hospitals and food production keep ticking over,” he added.
In a separate development, Zelenskyy thanked British Prime Minister Andy Burnham for a newly announced additional support package worth 10 billion pounds ($13.3bn) after a Wednesday morning phone call.
“A truly strong and very timely step – coming right as Russia needs to see and feel that Ukraine will not be left alone to deal with the problems Russia is so eager to escalate,” Zelenskyy wrote on social media.
According to Downing Street , the new British aid package for Ukraine includes 500 million pounds ($665m) in additional military support from the Ministry of Defence “to plug urgent gaps in Ukraine’s air defences this winter”.

items.title: Healey unveils £100 for energy bills and bank tax in first Budget
items.summary: The chancellor targets the cost of living amid global economic turmoil but opposition parties say he has not been bold enough.
items.content:
Millions of households will get Â£100 to help with soaring energy bills to be paid for by a tax on bank profits, John Healey has announced in his first Budget.
The chancellor said he wanted to give hard-pressed families "breathing space now" and "hope for the future" as the UK economy is battered by "global economic storms".
He also unveiled tax breaks to boost high street businesses - but confirmed that many big decisions, including on defence spending and welfare, will not be made until next year.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said Healey's plans were "not bold enough" and the government was "overspent, overborrowed, overtaxed and drowning in an out-of-control welfare system".
In an hour-long speech to a packed House of Commons, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham and other frontbench colleagues cheering him on, the chancellor unveiled a string of measures aimed at cutting the cost of living.
One-off Â£100 energy payment for people living in council tax bands A to D in England, with Wales saying it will match the payment and the Scottish government planning to "replicate" it
Gas standing charges in England, Scotland and Wales, to be scrapped during 2027 "or as soon as possible after". These fixed daily fees will be shifted onto the price of each unit of energy, meaning heavy gas users will face higher bills
Extending the 5p "temporary" cut in fuel duty on petrol and diesel to July
Increasing minimum wage rates by 3.9% in April, although there will be no progress on narrowing the gap between rates for older and younger workers
Healey increased the tax on the profits of big banks from 3% to 6%, which will last from January next year to April 2028, and increased taxes on high-stakes gambling machines.
Healey announces Â£100 energy bill help for millions and raises taxes on banks and some savers
Your pay, energy bills and savings: How the Budget affects you
Chris Mason: Budget felt cautious despite its range of small measures
As part of a package to help business, Healey increased the point at which High Street shops in England start paying business rates from Â£12,000 to Â£18,000, with vape shops and adult gaming centres excluded from the relief.
But he had little scope for big giveaways as the public finances remain stretched, with the UK set to spend Â£14bn more on debt interest payments this year.
Income tax thresholds will remain frozen and the tax on income from savings and property rental will rise to 24% for basic rate taxpayers from April 2027, after it had been scheduled to go up to 22%.
But a cut to the cash ISA allowance from Â£20,000 a year to Â£12,000, announced last year by Healey's predecessor Rachel Reeves, will be axed.
The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) downgraded its growth forecast for next year to 1%, with slightly higher increases predicted for subsequent years.
In its latest assessment, the OBR said British households were set to be little better off than before the Covid pandemic even a decade after Covid-19 hit, a situation the watchdog's boss David Miles described as "pretty grim".
In his Budget speech, Healey repeatedly stressed that the UK economy was being battered by "global uncertainties" and soaring oil prices caused by conflict in the Middle East.
"Those are the storms we face. We can't wish them away. We must choose the course we steer through them," he told MPs.
Figure caption, Watch: What are the key points from the Budget and how will it be funded?
Healey also used his speech to announce plans to allow regional mayors to keep 20% of business rates and a share of income tax to spend on local priorities.
The aim was to allow mayors to retain 100% of business rates raised in their areas by the end of the decade, he added, in "the most radical act of devolution in a generation".
And he sought to address opposition claims the Labour government is unwilling to cut benefits, insisting that both he and Burnham were committed to bringing down the welfare bill in a "Labour way".
But he said no decisions would be taken until reviews by Alan Milburn , into young people not in work or training, and Stephen Timms, on Personal Independence Payments , had been published, with legislation to follow next year.
The Â£4.7bn black hole in the defence investment plan will be funded, the chancellor revealed, in part through taking money from capital budgets across Whitehall.
Healey said he will set out how the government plans to meet its commitment to spend 3% of the national income on defence by 2030, and 3.5% by 2035, at next year's spending review.
But Badenoch said he "should have set out a plan for 3% today," highlighting his claim when he resigned as Sir Keir Starmer's defence secretary in June that UK forces were at risk due to a lack of cash.
"So now he is the man who is increasing risk to personnel on operations, he is the man who is making our country less safe, he has failed his own test," the Conservative leader said.
"This is on him and no-one will ever forget. If he had any decency he would resign again today."
The Tory leader said that with the UK heading for a record tax burden and "spending more on debt interest than on the army and schools combined", Healey's Budget was "not good enough, not strong enough, not bold enough".
Helen Miller, director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said the Budget "has a raft of fiddly measures but very little that will move the dial on growth".
Lib Dem leader Sir Ed Davey said that until the government has "the courage" to fix the UK's trading relationship with the EU any Budget will just be "tinkering around the edges" and will not provide the growth the country needs.
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the Budget was full of "little giveaways" but "doesn't overall do very much" and did not offer "anything of any value on defence whatsoever".
Healey also faced criticism from the left, with the general secretary of the Unite union, Sharon Graham describing the cost of living measures in the Budget as "baby steps".
"Scrapping standing charges on gas and a Â£100 energy payment for households in council tax bands, A to D, whilst welcome, will not touch the sides, when many forecasts show bills set to jump over Â£400 in January," she added.
Green Party leader Zack Polanski said it was a Budget "that betrays the future for young people and the planet they inherit".
He added: "The chancellor didn't mention climate once but praised bankers repeatedly."

U.S. Natural Gas Production Hits New Records as Demand Surges
U.S. natural gas production is set to hit consecutive records, reaching 112.2 Bcf/d in 2026 and a projected 116.1 Bcf/d in 2027.
Soaring LNG exports and AI data center demand are driving production growth, particularly in the Permian and Haynesville basins.
Producers are consolidating to capitalize on rising demand, highlighted by EQT's acquisition of Range Resources, while stronger output could push Henry Hub prices lower in 2027.
U.S. natural gas production is on track to close a second consecutive year with record-high natural gas output as producers respond to demand signs both at home and overseas.
Soaring demand for powering data centers in the United States and rising liquefied natural gas exports amid expanding liquefaction capacity, as well as surging global demand for spot LNG cargoes in the absence of Qatar’s gas due to the Iran war, are pushing American natural gas production higher this year.
Output is on track to beat in 2026 the record set in 2025 as more associated gas is being produced in the Permian basin along with oil, and operators boost gas output in the Haynesville basin, which is close to LNG export terminals and major domestic industrial gas users, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) says .
Rising production will more than offset higher LNG exports, resulting in an average Henry Hub spot price for natural gas of $3.16 per million British thermal units (MMBtu) in 2027, down by 9% compared to 2026, the EIA’s latest Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO) showed earlier this month.
For this year, U.S. dry natural gas production is set to jump to 112.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcfd) from 107.64 bcfd last year. In 2027, U.S. natural gas production is forecast to further grow to 116.13 bcfd to another record high, the EIA’s latest monthly estimates showed . Related: UBS Sees $110 Brent by Year-End as Gulf Flows Stay Below Prewar Levels
U.S. LNG exports averaged 17.4 billion cubic feet per day (Bcf/d) in the first six months of the year, 23% higher compared to the same period in 2025, as export capacity jumped and boosted shipments to the fastest pace since exports began a decade ago.
In the domestic market, data centers have turned to additional gas-fired power generation to support the booming AI market.
Amid rising gas demand, both in the U.S. and overseas, American gas producers are raising production and entering in strategic transactions to scale and expand.
Just this week, EQT Corporation and Range Resources announced a definitive merger agreement, under which EQT will buy Range in an all-stock transaction that will create America’s leading natural gas company with a pro-forma enterprise value over $50 billion.
“North American gas markets have shifted from producer-push to demand-pull, and this deal puts EQT firmly at the heart of that transition,” said Lydia Walker, Senior Research Analyst on Wood Mackenzie’s Lower 48 upstream team.
“Range cements EQT's position as the supplier of choice for Appalachian power generation and data centre growth, adding the scale, inventory and liquids diversification needed to serve that demand for decades to come,” Walker added.
A day later, EQT raised its 2026 production guidance by about 90 Bcfe, due to better-than-expected benefits from compression investments improving both existing and new wells and shallowing decline rates, while it reduced its full-year capital spending guidance by $25 million.
Thanks to “strong performance to date”, EQT also raised its full-year 2026 total sales volume guidance to 2,375 – 2,450 Bcfe.
Meanwhile, Range Resources raised its third-quarter natural gas production by 11% from a year earlier, and year-to-date output by 5% compared to January-September 2025.
“We have considerable momentum across our business and will be exiting 2026 in the strongest position in Range’s history,” CEO Dennis Degner said.
“With EQT, we will have improved market access, best-in-class inventory, enhanced cash flow generation, and fortified resiliency to drive profitable growth and shareholder value creation through commodity cycles.”
Expand Energy, currently the largest U.S. natural gas producer before the EQT-Range deal is completed early next year, said this week in the Q3 earnings release that it is positioning itself for a “historic wave of structural domestic demand growth” underway.
“A new era of demand-pull replaces historical supply-push dynamics across the U.S.,” Expand Energy said.

Treasury yields tick higher after Fed interest rate decision
Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) in New York City, U.S., August 4, 2026.
Bond yields moved higher on Wednesday as investors digested the Federal Reserve's decision to hold interest rates steady at its October meeting.
The 10-year Treasury note yield — the main benchmark for mortgages, auto loans and credit card debt — was more than 3 basis points higher at 5.026%.
The yield on the 2-year Treasury note, which more closely follows short-term Federal Reserve rate decisions, slipped more than 3 basis points to 4.704%.
The yield on longer-dated 30-year U.S. Treasury — which tend to move on geopolitical events — was also up by more than 4 basis points to 5.354%.
One basis point equals 0.01%, or 1/100th of 1%, and yields and prices move inversely to one another.
Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh said the bank remained focused on "price stability" despite the pause and that the employment picture has been "quite positive."
Despite the hold for October, expectations for a 25 basis points hike at the central bank's next meeting on Dec. 9 currently stand at 85.7%, according to CME's FedWatch tool.
More economic data is due Thursday. Personal consumption expenditures index — the Fed's preferred inflation gauge — as well as the quarterly GDP growth rate and personal income and spending data will offer investors additional insights into the domestic economy and inflation picture.
That data will be critical to determining where the Fed may go from here, according to TruStage chief economist Steve Rick.
"Holding rates steady doesn't necessarily mean the Fed is finished raising them, especially if inflation doesn't start to cool," he said. "Policymakers will want to see whether these price pressures are temporary or becoming more widespread throughout the economy."

UK vows defense spending will hit 3% of GDP by 2030
The U.K. set 2030 as the target for defense spending to reach 3% of GDP, while reaffirming it would meet the NATO commitment of 3.5% by 2035.
Finance minister John Healey announced an additional £10 billion in economic and military support for Ukraine, as well as urgent winter military funding.
Healey also outlined up to £5 billion for defense and dual-use investment and a £2.5 billion Rolls-Royce turbine technology partnership.
Britain's Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey holds the red Budget box outside 11 Downing Street ahead of the announcement of the Autumn Budget in the House of Commons in London, United Kingdom on October 28, 2026.
Wiktor Szymanowicz | Future Publishing | Getty Images
The U.K. has set out a target date for defense spending to rise to 3% of GDP, as the finance minister announced billions in aid for Ukraine in a "clear message to Moscow".
John Healey on Wednesday set a target date of 2030 for the 3% figure, while reaffirming its NATO commitment to reach 3.5% by 2035 .
Healey, who resigned as defense minister under the previous government over insufficient spending, presented his first annual budget as finance minister and highlighted a "new era of threat".
"Today we send a clear message to Moscow: Britain will stand with Ukraine for as long as it takes," he said as he announced an additional £10 billion ($13.3 billion) in economic and military support, based on loans, export finance guarantees, as well as £500 million in urgent military funding for this winter.
The government will set out the details of how it will meet its defense spending targets at the spending review next year, Healey told lawmakers.
"As we look ahead to the spending review, we start from a position of strength, with spending at that higher base, there will be choices we have to make about priorities," he said.
"Today, I'm getting work underway to get there in a fiscally sustainable way," Healey said against the backdrop of strained public finances and increasing borrowing costs.

Healey also said the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank will deploy up to £5 billion over the next four years into defence, dual-use technologies and other sectors supporting national security to strengthen the UK defense industrial base, support domestic supply chains and attract private investment.
Chris Beauchamp, chief UK market analyst at investing and trading platform IG, said Healey's announcement lacked detail but "it looks like defence will get the money Healey said was needed when he was defence secretary."
"The precise path will come through next year, but it seems like the spending bonanza for Rolls-Royce and others is still on the way. It just might take a little while to arrive," he added.
Healey also announced that Rolls-Royce will develop its next-generation turbine engine technology in partnership with the U.K. government, in an investment worth £2.5 billion.

Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia all traveled to Tehran to meet President Masoud Pezeshkian and other Iranian leaders Image: Iranian Presidency/AFP Advertisement
Amid rising fear that the US and Israel are preparing to launch new attacks on Iran after the US midterm election  on November 3, three major Middle Eastern powers delivered a coordinated diplomatic message directly to Tehran.
Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir , Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin all traveled to Iran to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior officials in Tehran this Monday. The three envoys serve as representatives for the Mecca defense pact — a military alliance of Islamabad, Riyad and Ankara, which was officially set up this summer.
Saudi Arabia said ⁠the ⁠trip aims to open negotiating channels and "prevent the return of military escalation." Details on the agenda, however, remain scarce.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
A senior Pakistani  official cited by the Reuters news agency said the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network, in addition to US-Iran talks, Houthi rebels ' attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade.
Another official said Pakistan's Munir presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something both to Washington and Iran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar acting as mediators. The source told Reuters US President Donald Trump previously gave Munir the go-ahead to try diplomacy.
Iran hailed the "very positive atmosphere" during the Tehran talks, even though no breakthroughs were officially announced.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region."
Rezaei argued that regional security should be built by countries in West Asia themselves and without outside intervention.
A day later, Rezaei reportedly met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media said Khamenei called for protecting Iran's interests and maintaining Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current state of "neither war nor peace."
Meanwhile, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian travelled to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, with Pezeshkian and the emir also discussing the war and the Strait of Hormuz.
These and other diplomatic contacts were framed by Tehran as evidence that the US is unable to diplomatically isolate the Iranian regime.
Are Turkey and Pakistan closing ranks with Saudi Arabia?
The united front presented by the three nations in Tehran, however, can also be seen as a show of force for the new Mecca defense alliance. It comes as the Saudis grow increasingly wary of  the attacks on Saudi infrastructure launched by the Iran-allied Houthi militants .
Egypt ready to back Saudi Arabia's war against Houthis
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Under the terms of the Mecca agreement, an outside attack on one of the member states is to be regarded as an attack on all of them. The visit also came on the same day as Egypt's parliament agreeing to give military help to Ryad and take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, in addition to the looming threat of the US and Israel.
"The presence of the three senior representatives at the same time sent the message that these countries are acting as a bloc," Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW.
Saudi Arabia has long been regarded as Iran's archrival in region. It has used its enormous wealth to counter Iran's influence, and now it can, at least in theory, also count on Pakistan's nuclear capability, and Turkey's conventional military strength.
At the same time, Dorbeiki argued that the Mecca pact is primarily designed for deterrence rather than offensive war. And having a defense pact does not mean its members want to fight Iran.
Dorbeiki believes the message from the bloc could therefore work in two directions: It can provide mediation, but continued escalation could also alter that position.
Saudi Arabia faces the most immediate dilemma. Further Houthi attacks have damaged its infrastructure and economy , but a wider war with Iran could threaten the investment and development projects at the heart of Riyadh's economic strategy.
"For Saudi Arabia, both the current situation and a war with Iran carry serious costs," Dorbeiki said. "Its preferred route is, therefore, a diplomatic solution."
What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack?
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
Moreover, Pakistan has spent months mediating between Washington and Tehran , and has important relations with both. A direct conflict would also distract Islamabad from its long-standing security concerns involving India.
Turkey is a NATO member, but Dorbeiki said direct military support for Iran against the United States is highly improbable. The fact that Ankara sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin rather than its foreign or defense minister also suggests a cautious approach.
Iran pursues diplomacy while preparing for fighting
Ali Asghar Shafieian, media advisor for Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, also rejected the perspective that the Mecca pact representatives were trying to present Tehran with an ultimatum.
He told DW that the three countries may also have wanted to demonstrate their own growing coordination, while showing that Iran remains part of regional diplomacy.
"You cannot conclude from this meeting alone that it was an ultimatum before an attack," Shafieian said.
He also noted that Iran, just like the US and Israel, could prepare for the possibility of further conflict while maintaining negotiations.
Mediator or enforcer? Pakistan's role in the Middle East
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
"Just as they use the opportunity to strengthen their military and defensive capabilities, Iran does the same," he said, adding that an agreement remains possible if Iran's political standing and what Tehran describes as its national dignity are respected.
Dorbeiki argued that Iran is following a familiar strategy of extending negotiations while avoiding real-world commitments.
The Houthi rebels are central to Tehran's calculation.
Tehran has not publicly offered the kind of guarantees over Houthi attacks that Riyadh would want. Dorbeiki believes Iran could seek to trade influence over such the attacks for concessions such as an end to US military pressure and broader steps toward ending the war.
The only apparent outcome of the Tehran meeting is to keep talking. For Iran, that might be enough of a signal that it is still a diplomatic partner rather than an enemy.

Trump says Iran war will end 'when I want it to' as costs balloon
Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.
His statement comes as a report from The Hill revealed that the costs of the Iran conflict have ballooned to $47 billion.
The war is costing American families about $2,000 more since it started, according to Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics.
US President Donald Trump speaks to the media before boarding Air Force One at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland on Oct. 27, 2026.
U.S. President Donald Trump has reiterated his claim that the Iran war will end "whenever I want it to," but insists that Tehran cannot have a nuclear weapon.
Speaking at a rally in Lubbock, Texas, Trump said "Somebody asked me before, 'When will the war in Iran end?' I said, 'Whenever I want it to end.'"
Trump said it "would be very quick, but we have to have an end properly ," with a "total statement" that Iran would never have a nuclear weapon.
His statement comes as the president grapples with poll numbers that are near a record low due to rising energy costs and affordability issues as the U.S. heads into the midterm elections on Nov. 3.
Currently, Trump's approval ratings stand at 32%, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll on Monday.
Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's Analytics, said on Oct. 12 that the war was costing American families an average of $2,000 so far, where $1,100 comes from higher energy costs, $540 from heightened interest rate costs and $360 due to increased military spending.
The Iran conflict shows no sign of winding down, with Trump saying that he will soon decide whether to "make a deal" with Iran or "finish it off."
Earlier in the month, the U.S. had evacuated diplomats from Saudi Arabia, as The New York Times reported that U.S. and Israeli militaries have drawn up specific plans for a "short but intensive" operation for strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.
An estimate by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 16, according to a report by The Hill, also revealed that the cost of the Iran war has ballooned to $47 billion, about $3 billion more than the previous numbers.
The bulk of the costs was reportedly for munitions replacements at $29 billion. Washington's conflict with Iran has caused "shortfalls" in U.S. munitions, despite Trump claiming on Sept. 3 that the U.S. had "virtually unlimited" amounts of ammunition.
The massive price tag on the war does not include the costs of damaged military bases in the Middle East, which is estimated at $184 million as of June 29, according to a lead inspector general report to Congress.
This figure counts damage to U.S. diplomatic facilities in four countries — Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — from Iranian strikes.

items.summary: Iran rejects 'unacceptable' proposal by Qatar to end war with US  Middle East Eye
items.content:
Iran has rejected a proposal from Qatar to end the US -led war on the country, calling it "unacceptable".
Qatar presented the draft deal, which would look to end the eight-month conflict, to Iranian negotiators on Sunday.
However, a senior Iranian official told Reuters on Wednesday that his country could not work with what had been presented, adding that Tehran would show no flexibility regarding the nuclear issue.
US Vice President JD Vance said earlier this month that Iran must reduce nuclear enrichment to end the war. The Islamic Republic has repeatedly stated that its nuclear programme is entirely for non-military domestic use.
The negotiations come amid mounting fears that the US and Israel could imminently resume their attacks on Iran.
Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, in particular, has been touting the prospect of new attacks as he seeks re-election in Israel's parliamentary elections .
With 77 percent of votes counted, Netanyahu's bloc is the largest in the Israeli parliament.
On Wednesday, as negotiations were set to begin on forming a new government, Netanyahu announced he would work with US President Donald Trump to eliminate the "existential threat" posed by Iran.
His main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has also supported strikes on Iran in tandem with economic pressure.
The Israel-US war on Iran has, since it began in February, caused massive disruption to the global economy, sending energy prices soaring.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned on Wednesday that any Israeli-instigated attack in the Gulf region would have a "devastating impact" on global markets.
"Devastating impact on int'l markets of any Israel-instigated military misadventure in Persian Gulf region remains major concern for both gas suppliers and consumers," Araghchi said in a post on X.
'Escalation is coming': Middle East on edge as new Israeli-US attack on Iran looms
The fallout of any renewed conflict in the Gulf would also be compounded by the ongoing fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-aligned Houthis in Yemen .
The Houthis, officially named Ansar Allah, on Wednesday called for the evacuation of the airport in Aden, the city in southern Yemen that serves as the seat of the Saudi-backed government.
"Our armed forces call on those present at Aden Airport to evacuate the premises immediately, due to the presence of a Saudi military cargo plane carrying weapons intended to kill the Yemeni people," Houthi spokesperson Yahya Saree wrote on X.
Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed forces in Yemen has seen nearly 100 fighters killed since Monday, military sources from both sides told AFP.
At least 63 Houthi fighters and 34 combatants associated with the internationally recognised government died, mostly near the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
